name: The Wright household
head: wright_john

arrival.note: Both men, same year, stated twice.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Two named Wrights arrive in 1832 and are grouped here as one household. Whether a mother or other children travelled with them is not stated.

origin.note: A CAME-FROM AND NOT A BIRTHPLACE, WHICH IS THE CLAIM THIS FIELD ACTUALLY ASKS FOR. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 89 (claim bk_mose1_001): "Among these in 1832 were Philo Carpenter, and John S. Wright from Massachusetts; T. W. Goodrich, Hamilton Barnes, Dr. Philip Maxwell from New York; Dr. E. S. Kimberly, George W. Snow, of Vermont, and Alanson Sweet." The sentence is about men who CAME THROUGH CHICAGO IN 1832 AND DECIDED TO REMAIN, so the state is attached to the coming and not to a birth — which is what separates it from the Calumet Club roll's birthplaces that most of this layer's cited origins rest on. THE DRAWN BLOCK IS RETIRED BY ITS OWN TERMS: it carried `replaceable_by` "a source that says where this household came from", and this is that source, so the draw's basis, seed and stage mark go with it. Graded `inferred` and never higher — an 1895 compilation, transcription_mediated, crediting Andreas and Hurlbut on the pages read here (the ceiling T-1322 set for the settlers table in the same volume). THE HOUSEHOLD TAKES THE SON'S STATED ORIGIN BECAUSE THE TWO CAME TOGETHER: this card's own arrival note says "Both men, same year, stated twice", John Wright and his son John S. Wright arriving in 1832 as one party, so where they came from is one answer and the compiler gives it for the one of them he names. The draw had said New York State.

reason_for_coming.value: A store for the traffic of a town filling up
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as merchant, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

basis.note: arrival_fill.trade_reasons.a_store_for_the_traffic — the head's recorded trade is evidence about this household, and the draw it answered is the reason the record will carry until a source states one.

works_at.note: NOT MODELLED. Wright's store is documented by his own advertisement of November 1833 and has no record in data/structures/, so there is nothing to link to. A second gap from the same advertisement: the TWO BUILDINGS he had to let are two more documented structures with no records, and they are evidence about the town's rental housing stock, which is otherwise invisible.

present_on_scene_date.note: John S. Wright's later Chicago career is continuous; the father is not followed past 1833 in anything reached, which is why the household is present on inference rather than on a statement.

persons.name: John Wright

occupation.note: 'John Wright, came in 1832, a merchant'. His advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 offers cut nails and general merchandise, and he separately advertises TWO BUILDINGS TO LET until 1 June 1834 - which makes him the only documented landlord of rental property in this parcel.

workplaces.basis: The register matches the printed name to the town card wright_john (action: enrich), so this is the same person the resident layer already holds. Dated by the printing window, which bounds the reading and does not date the partnership.

persons.note: ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 1833 (Andreas prints the poll: 'John W. Wright'), one of the twenty-eight electors five days later, a candidate who took two votes, and one of the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago in August 1833, at the funeral of a child. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds, and an advertisement in it is a peculiarly good witness: the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. It is also NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, so it is strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835.

resident_research.evidence_against: 'John Wright' at printed page 207 line 17 (33SQ-GYYJ-93G) is NOT 'John S. Wright': The name 'John Wright' is borne by 2 person(s) of 1835 and appears on 1 named 1840 head line(s). A name that two people share cannot identify either of them, so the pair is refused by measurement rather than by anyone's list of common names. L5 name_is_not_unique The surname 'Wright' is in Norris 1844 and no entry under it carries the initial 'J' of 'John Wright'. A surname-only agreement is a refusal. The same volume's obituary list prints 'Wright, John, died September 20, 1810, aged 57' — a death 25 years before the scene date, so that entry is not this man; the 1840 census pair is refused in the repository because 'John Wright' is borne by two people of 1835.
resident_research.summary: Corroborated in a volume printed after the scene date. John Wright agrees with an entry in the Fergus 1839/1843 and Norris 1844 directories, the old-settler rolls and Fergus's death notices. The reading enriches the biography and adds no 1835 attestation.
resident_research.notes: Research only. Later-volume readings are recorded here and NOT promoted: T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply.

merge_ruling.for_merge: A dropped r, and the initial J agrees with John Wright the merchant — the 1833 poll and tax lists, the Democrat of 26 November 1833 and 25 February 1834, the 1840 census at 207:17.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE INITIAL J HAS TWO RIVALS AMONG THE WRIGHTS AND THE `wright` CLUSTER HAS ALREADY SAID SO. Its standing U1/R2 ruling refuses a bare 'J. Wright' because the father and the son share the forename John and the initial cannot choose between them; folding the surname as well adds a third candidate and removes nothing. 'J. F. Wight' is one reading, the Democrat of 11 June 1834 (#c007), and its middle initial F is carried by no Wright of this town — John S. Wright's is S, and T-0997's C2 merge inside that cluster turned on exactly that printed letter. The town holds six Wright cards and one Wight. Refused by a ratified rule; no ballot needed.

merge_ruling.for_merge: 'J. Wright' in the American of 11 July 1835 is a Wright in the town in the scene year.
merge_ruling.against_merge: The initial J has two rivals — the father and the son, who share a forename. R2 refuses. Refused by a ratified rule; no ballot needed.

No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('wright_john:age_bands_1840'). The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

persons.name: John S. Wright

occupation.note: NO TRADE IS RECORDED FOR HIM IN 1833-35 and this value is a reconstruction. Andreas calls him 'John S. Wright, then a minor, afterward editor of Prairie Farmer, and one of the most meritorious pioneers of Chicago, came in 1832'. A minor in his merchant father's business is a clerk on the ordinary reading of the period; the source says only that he was young and that he came.

dated_bounds.note: AN APPEARANCE IN THE TOWN'S PRINT, AND NOTHING FURTHER. The Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-29 names 'J. S. Wright' in the claim read as chicago_democrat_1834_10_29#c006, so the reading dates an appearance of this person in the town's press and `here_by` is null: a name in print is not a body in the town, and a notice can be signed elsewhere and reprinted here. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the issue is deposited, dated and numbered in data/research/newspapers/corpus.json, and what no source states is that the name the paper prints is the person on this card — the register joins them under its own written note. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: A MINOR IN 1833 AND A FOUNDING MEMBER OF THE FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN JUNE OF THAT YEAR - his name is in the list of nine village citizens alongside his father's. He would have been about twenty in 1835. THE RELATIONSHIP IS THIS RECORD'S READING: Andreas lists the two Wrights separately and never says they are father and son, and 'John Wright, came in 1832, a merchant' and 'John S. Wright, then a minor ... came in 1832' arriving in the same year with the same surname and joining the same church on the same day is a strong reading and not a statement.

research_note: A FATHER-AND-SON HOUSEHOLD ASSEMBLED FROM TWO SEPARATE ROSTER ENTRIES, and one of only three multi-generation households in this parcel. THE ADVERTISEMENT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE PEOPLE HERE: 'Two Buildings to Let' until 1 June 1834 documents a rental market in a town of perhaps a thousand people, and this project holds a trap about that same advertisement - it carries an engraving of a three-storey building which is a jobbing printer's stock cut and NOT a picture of anything in Chicago.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. wright_john, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1647 (a single entry); wright_john_s, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1648 (a single entry); wright_john_s, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e2675 (a single entry).

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Wright, John, Michigan ave. cor. Madison st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. Michigan Avenue is the lakefront street south of the river and is NOT the 1835 layer's Michigan Street, which runs east from La Salle on the north side. Two streets, one word, and the 1839 directory prints both. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause 3).

back_projection.note: A LATER ADDRESS, READ BACKWARDS 4 YEARS. The door is not an 1835 reading: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 printed it in 1839, and this pass carries it back to the scene date because the 1835 record attests a trade for this person and nothing in the corpus places it better. What is claimed is the street face and nothing narrower — no lot, no roof, no door count — and the grade is `reconstructed`, which is this dataset's word for a figure the reconstruction supplies rather than a source. North Water Street stands in 1835 under that name and in that place. The directory gives a street and nothing this pass can resolve narrower, so the placement is the FACE — the unit the owner's ruling of 2026-08-29 says a street name constrains — and no roof is dealt. The rule this stands on is docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md and the liberty is L218; a reader who thinks 4 years is too far to carry a shop should read the grade as the disagreement being invited.
